thread:
nina: Hey team, escalating a Private/VPC customer issue — they're seeing intermittent 429s from our customer-managed gateway after a short burst of traffic. Customer says it used to be fine; they moved some traffic behind an ingress controller change last week. Logs attached (pasted below).

nina: customer logs (sanitized):
```
2026-03-10T11:02:14Z WARN rate_limiter: rate_exceeded key=acct-123 limit=100 rps burst=20
2026-03-10T11:02:14Z ERROR gateway: 429 "rate limit" route=/v1/generate api_key=redacted src_ip=10.1.5.7
2026-03-10T11:02:15Z INFO cache: kv_hit prefix=common_prompt
```

nina: Repro notes from customer: they spin up a small spike (~350 reqs/s for ~6s) using a load runner against the ingress. After the spike, 429s persist for ~30s even though backend pods have capacity. They suspect a leaky-bucket token refill or ingress-level queuing. They provided their k8s ingress annotations (they're using nginx-ingress):
```
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-rps: "100"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-burst: "20"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/enable-owasp-core-rules: "true"
```

ramos: Thanks @nina — couple quick Qs: is this happening for all customers in that VPC or a single account? Are we seeing token consumption matching the customer's account in our billing logs?

nina: Single customer. We do see a short spike in usage in our internal usage logs for acct-123 at the same time window; the spike amount matches their generator. Billing counters don't show long-term overage — usage returned to baseline quickly. The 429s are returned by the customer-managed gateway, not our hosted API.

chris: My guess: nginx-ingress limit-rps is per-source IP by default (client IP) unless configured for X-Forwarded-For. If the load generator is coming through a NAT/Gateway the source IP could appear as the same and hit a global limit. But nina said 429s continue after backend recovers — that sounds like a token-bucket refill period on the ingress controller or an external rate-limit service with a short cooldown.

ada: Also check whether the gateway uses an external rate limit service (envoy external ratelimit or redis-backed limiter). If the limiter stores buckets in redis with TTL or uses a global fixed window, bursts can cause subsequent requests to be dropped until counters reset.

nina: Customer uses an Envoy-based customer gateway behind a GCE/LB. They added a sidecar redis rate-limiter (rls) — config snippet they sent: 
```
ratelimit:
  domain: redwood_gateway
  descriptors:
    - key: "api_key"
      value: "{request.headers['x-api-key']}"
      rate_limit:
        requests_per_unit: 100
        unit: second
  redis:
    socket: /var/run/redis/redis.sock
    prefix: rls:acct-123
```
jenny: That descriptor is per-second with requests_per_unit=100 — if the spike is 350 rps, tokens will be exhausted. Check whether they set a burst/bucket_size param. Many rls setups have a separate "burst_multiplier" or explicit burst size.

ramos: Also important: is the limit keyed on api_key or on client IP? If the ingress rewrites X-Forwarded-For and we have a shared NAT, many clients look like one source. The customer mentioned they route through an internal NAT for outgoing test traffic.

nina: They confirmed it's keyed on api_key (above config). They also said they recently changed the nginx ingress controller to use the "global" rate-limit feature rather than per-virtualhost due to a cert rotation; maybe that introduced a shared limiter.

ops-bot: @channel automated note: we have a support ticket open (#SUP-8421) and a linked incident draft (INC-2026-03-10-rls-burst).

chris: Suggested immediate triage steps for customer:
- Run kubectl describe on the ingress and ratelimit pods to confirm the applied annotation and running config.
- Check redis keys for rls prefix to see bucket state: `redis-cli keys "rls:acct-123*"` and `redis-cli get rls:acct-123:<descriptor>`
- Reproduce with a controlled load tool (hey/vegeta) and capture timestamps to see when tokens are depleted and when they refill.

ada: I'll add a couple of commands to dump envoy rls calls: enable debug logging for the rate limit sidecar and tail logs: `kubectl -n gateway logs -l app=ratelimit -f` and `kubectl -n gateway exec -it ratelimit-xxx -- redis-cli --raw GET rls:acct-123`

nina: Customer ran `redis-cli TTL rls:acct-123:descriptor1` and saw TTL=27s during the hit window. That matches the ~30s 429 tail-off. So the limiter uses TTL to enforce a cooldown.

ramos: That explains the persistent 429s after the spike. Two mitigation paths: 1) increase bucket size/burst, 2) change strategy to token refill with smaller TTL / sliding window, or 3) implement a short-term internal allowlist for known test IPs.

jenny: For Kubernetes nginx-ingress there's also `limit-rps` and `limit-burst` annotations — but if they replaced per-host with global limiter the global limiter may be applying more strict semantics (e.g., fixed window counters). Recommend updating rls config so descriptor includes a smaller granularity (per-second with sliding window) and explicit `burst: 200` if they expect spikes.

nina: Customer asked about coaching on safe values. They have baseline 40 rps steady, occasional peak 350 rps for <10s. For a token-bucket, a conservative burst of ~400 with refill_rate=100 should avoid 429s for 10s peaks. Also ensure the Redis TTL is low (<=1s) for sliding-window behavior rather than long cooldowns.

chris: Also worth considering layering: have the ingress accept the spike and let the Redwood private control plane (customer's rate limit config in our platform) do fine-grain per-api-key enforcement rather than the gateway killing everything. But since this is customer-managed gateway, we need them to tune their rls.

ada: Repro steps we documented and sent to customer (they confirmed):
1) baseline: run `hey -c 50 -q 10 -z 30s https://gw.customer.internal/v1/generate` (expect baseline stable)
2) burst: `hey -c 350 -q 0 -z 6s https://gw.customer.internal/v1/generate` -> observe 429s start around t0+2s
3) post-burst: run a low-rate test `hey -c 5 -q 1 -z 20s` and watch for 429s to persist for ~TTL seconds in redis.

nina: Customer applied the recommended temporary fix: increased rls descriptor burst to 400 and reduced TTL to 1s. They reported downstream clients no longer see prolonged 429 tail for short bursts. They asked whether we should recommend any RBAC/auth changes — they use API key header `x-api-key` and we recommended to avoid using source IP as primary key when requests pass through NAT.

ramos: Follow-up asks for our runbook: we should add a KB article for Private customers: "Configuring RLS for bursty workloads" with examples for nginx-ingress and Envoy rls, include recommended burst/refill TTL examples, and how to inspect redis keys to correlate 429 tail. Also include a sample vegeta/hey repro script.

ada: I'll draft the KB and post in #docs once we have an ops-approved template. Key points to cover: per-key vs per-ip limits, burst sizing strategy, TTL behavior for redis-backed limiters, and verifying with redis-cli + kubectl logs.

chris: Closing notes for ticket: root cause = customer-managed redis-backed rate limiter configured with per-second limit=100 and TTL ~30s + no burst allowance; after spike tokens are exhausted and key TTL caused 30s cooldown -> persistent 429s. Remediation = increase burst/bucket size and/or change to sliding-window token refill (TTL=1s), ensure limiter keys are per-api-key, and confirm ingress annotations for limit-burst if using nginx.

nina: Customer confirmed fix worked and will keep the longer-term change (sliding window and burst) in their infra repo. They'll also add a postmortem in their internal change log about the ingress change that triggered the behavior.

ops-bot: Support ticket #SUP-8421 updated: status -> resolved; notes added: apply rls burst and TTL changes.

ramos: Thanks @nina and @ada. I'll add the ticket summary to the Private deployment support digest for next week's sync. :thumbsup:

nina: posting final repro commands and sample redis debug snippet into the KB draft.

support-bot: Automated reminder: please set the external-facing KB to "customer-visible" only after legal review for on-prem configs.

nina: ack.
